title: Design WhatsApp

context.problem: A real-time messaging service: 1:1 and small-group text plus media, delivered in under half a second while both parties are online, queued reliably for 30 days when they are not, synchronised across a user's devices, with presence. Mobile networks are assumed unreliable.
constraints: messages deleted from servers after delivery
group size capped at 100 to bound fan-out

functional.text: Multi-device sync via per-device high-water mark

nonFunctional.target: no acknowledged loss on process, node, zone, or ordinary promotion; regional disaster RPO <5 min
nonFunctional.rationale: delivery guarantee is the product, scoped by failure domain
causality within a chat is what users notice

priorities.rationale: 500M DAU stated; an acknowledged message may never be lost

conflicts.resolution: at-least-once transport + client-side dedup by message id

assumptions.text: 20 messages sent per user per day
10% of messages carry media, ~200 KB average
5% of messages await an offline recipient, ~2-day mean wait

rows.derivation: 10B × 1 KB = 10 TB/day; active = 5% undelivered × 2-day mean wait ≈ 1 TB; 30-day retention ceiling = 300 TB
one recipient lookup per message; must be sub-ms → in-memory registry

invariants: membership is checked before accepting a send

entities.name: Message
entities.purpose: An immutable user-authored event with delivery state tracked separately.
invariants: a client message id is unique per sender device
an acknowledgement is emitted only after durable acceptance

entities.name: Device inbox
entities.purpose: The durable per-device backlog and resume cursor.
invariants: a reconnect cannot skip an accepted message

entities.purpose: A short-lived mapping from a device to its current gateway.

entities.name: Conversation
entities.representation: Not a stored aggregate — a partition key. Membership and group metadata are rows in the authoritative User/group DB; the conversation's content uses one durable acceptance partition in flight and a keyed row range in the message store at rest.
entities.identity: conversationId, minted once and stable for the life of the chat; it is also the partition key everywhere the conversation appears
entities.orderingAuthority: The candidate's durable acceptance partition for this conversationId. Its committed sequence is the conversation's one logical order — no component outside it may assign sequence.
entities.conflictResolution: Single-writer: the User/group DB is the only authority for membership, and the send path reads it and rejects a non-member before anything is accepted. Concurrent membership edits serialize there.
entities.durabilityPoint: The User/group DB commit for membership. A conversation holds no other state that can be lost.
entities.gc: The conversation record outlives its messages. Retiring it is a membership deletion, never a partition deletion — dropping the partition would let a late arrival be ordered against nothing.

entities.name: Message
entities.representation: An immutable event. In flight it is a record in the conversation's durable acceptance partition; at rest it is a row keyed (conversationId, messageId) in the wide-row message store. Media never travels in the message — the body carries a reference to an object in storage.
entities.identity: A server-assigned messageId. The sender's clientMessageId, scoped to the sending device, is the deduplication key that makes a retried send idempotent.
entities.orderingAuthority: The conversation's durable acceptance partition. Wall clocks are not consulted, and there is no global sequencer.
entities.conflictResolution: None is needed for the message itself — it is append-only and never mutates. Delivery state moves as a separate receipt, resolved by max-state transition (sent < delivered < read), so a reordered or duplicated receipt can never move it backwards.
entities.durabilityPoint: The durable acceptance-partition commit. That commit is also the sender's acknowledgement — there is no window in which the sender has seen an ack that the system could still lose under the scoped failure promise.
entities.gc: Delivered messages are deleted from servers after delivery. Undelivered ones are parked in the authoritative message store on a 30-day clock, not held in the acceptance partition: transient authority transfers to the store before the partition's retention window closes.

entities.name: Device inbox
entities.representation: A derived per-device backlog materialized from accepted messages plus an authoritative resume cursor in the message store. The backlog is rebuildable and is never the authority for message content.
entities.identity: (deviceId, conversationId). Each cursor is the highest acceptedSequence that this device has acknowledged receiving in that conversation; there is deliberately no cross-conversation cursor.
entities.orderingAuthority: Borrowed. The inbox imposes no order of its own; it drains each conversation's committed sequence in order and interleaves across conversations arbitrarily.
entities.conflictResolution: Monotonic max. A cursor only moves forward, so a stale reconnect carrying a lower cursor is discarded rather than applied — the cost of the rule is redelivery, which client-side dedup by clientMessageId already absorbs.
entities.durabilityPoint: The per-conversation cursor advance must be durable in the message store before the corresponding backlog entry may be dropped; the write ordering is what makes a reconnect unable to skip an accepted message.
entities.gc: A backlog entry drops once every one of the user's device cursors has passed it, or at the 30-day retention ceiling, whichever comes first.

entities.name: Connection lease
entities.representation: An expiring entry in the in-memory connection registry mapping deviceId to the gateway currently holding its socket. Derived, sized at roughly 5 GB fleet-wide, and deliberately never persisted.
entities.identity: deviceId plus device session id, so exactly one lease is active per device session and a reconnect supersedes rather than duplicates.
entities.orderingAuthority: The presence service, which renews leases from gateway heartbeats. Recency is the order that matters — the newest heartbeat is by definition the live connection.
entities.conflictResolution: Last writer wins on heartbeat recency. An expired lease is treated as absent, and a routing miss is not an error: it falls through to the device inbox, which is the durable path.
entities.durabilityPoint: None, by choice. Losing the entire registry costs a wave of redelivery from device inboxes, not a lost message — which is why presence is allowed to be fast and lossy.
entities.gc: TTL expiry on heartbeat timeout — a 30-second heartbeat with a 60-second reap. A gateway drain expires its leases explicitly instead of waiting for the timeout.

schemas.name: Message
notes: Immutable after acceptance; delivery receipts are stored separately.

schemas.name: Conversation
indexes: memberId — conversations visible to a user
notes: Membership is checked before a message is accepted.

schemas.name: DeviceInbox
indexes: (deviceId, conversationId, acceptedSequence) — reconnect range scan after each cursor
notes: Entries expire after delivery or the 30-day offline retention ceiling.

schemas.name: DeviceResumeCursor
indexes: (deviceId, conversationId) — one resume position per conversation
notes: Advance by max only; commit before deleting matching inbox entries.
Ordering is per conversation, never global — cross-conversation order is not a product promise, and no candidate buys one.

Every consumer on the delivery path is at-least-once, so every write is idempotent by clientMessageId within its conversation. Deduplication is the price paid for refusing to claim exactly-once delivery.

The split between authoritative and derived is the spine: A's queue and B's log are transient authority until authoritative message-store commit and consumer acknowledgement; device inboxes and the connection registry remain rebuildable views.

Rejected alternative C — Cell-based isolation: write-behind acknowledges from the in-memory grid before durable persistence, so an ordinary cell crash can lose acknowledged messages inside the zero-loss failure scope.

interfaces.name: Connect or resume
interfaces.purpose: Authenticate a device, install its connection lease, and drain missed messages.
interfaces.deadline: 5 s to authenticate and return the accepted per-conversation cursors
interfaces.retryability: reconnect with the same device session id and last accepted per-conversation cursors
interfaces.backpressure: gateway closes overloaded sessions with 1013; device reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter
interfaces.compatibility: additive command fields within protocol v1; ignore unknown fields
interfaces.failureResult: CONNECTED with accepted cursors; REJECTED with auth or cursor error; UNKNOWN on timeout after session installation—reconnect with the same session id

interfaces.name: Send message
interfaces.purpose: Durably accept a message before acknowledging the sender.
interfaces.retryability: retry with the same clientMessageId after reconnect
interfaces.backpressure: server overload closes with 1013; client reconnects with jitter
interfaces.compatibility: additive fields only within v1; ignore unknown fields
interfaces.failureResult: ACCEPTED with messageId; REJECTED before commit; UNKNOWN if the gateway deadline expires after the durable acceptance-partition commit may have occurred

interfaces.name: Update receipt
interfaces.purpose: Advance delivery state without rewriting the immutable message.
interfaces.deadline: 2 s to accept the receipt update
interfaces.retryability: retry any timeout; duplicate or older states are no-ops
interfaces.backpressure: coalesce pending receipts to the highest state per message and pause sends while the socket is unwritable
interfaces.compatibility: new receipt states require a negotiated protocol version; unknown optional fields are ignored
interfaces.failureResult: APPLIED, NO_OP, or REJECTED; UNKNOWN on timeout is resolved by retrying the same monotonic transition

interfaces.name: Request media upload
interfaces.purpose: Mint a short-lived direct-to-object-storage upload URL.
interfaces.trustBoundary: authenticated sender device → media API; upload then crosses to object storage
interfaces.deadline: 2 s to return an upload URL
interfaces.retryability: retry 429 and 5xx with the same upload request id; do not retry other 4xx responses
interfaces.backpressure: 429 with Retry-After; client limits concurrent upload requests to two
interfaces.compatibility: versioned /v1 path; response fields are additive and unknown fields are ignored
interfaces.failureResult: CREATED with uploadId and a URL valid for 15 min; RATE_LIMITED or REJECTED; UNKNOWN on timeout after creation—retry the same upload request id

deepDives.title: Make the acknowledgement point the durability point
deepDives.pressure: 463k peak sends/s and no acknowledged-message loss
deepDives.decision: Acknowledge only after the partitioned message log commits; persistence and delivery consume independently.
alternatives: queue then synchronously write message history
deepDives.failureMode: a gateway or consumer dies after the sender sees an acknowledgement

deepDives.title: Recover socket routing without treating presence as durable truth
deepDives.pressure: 50M concurrent mobile connections with reconnects and gateway deploys
deepDives.decision: Use expiring device-to-gateway leases, heartbeats, and inbox replay from the device cursor after reconnect.
deepDives.failureMode: a stale lease routes a message to a dead gateway

deepDives.title: Bound ordering and duplicate suppression
deepDives.pressure: retries, multiple devices, and cross-region delivery make global order impossible
deepDives.decision: Partition by conversation for causal order and deduplicate with sender-device client message ids.
deepDives.failureMode: a retry creates a duplicate or clock skew reorders a conversation

architectures.name: Service-based with async delivery spine
architectures.thesis: Coarse stateless services behind persistent-connection gateways; a queue decouples acknowledgement from delivery; one wide-row store owns messages.

pros: durability and ordering are properties of the log, not of worker code
463k peak msg/s is routine for a partitioned log; consumers scale per concern
replay gives crash recovery, backfill, and new features (search index) for free
peak smoothing: 4x bursts absorb into consumer lag, not dropped messages
cons: highest operational skill floor: partitions, offsets, consumer groups, lag monitoring
end-to-end latency is a sum of produce + two consume hops — budget carefully against 500 ms
nondeterministic event paths are harder to test than request/response

reasoning: Both candidates close the acknowledged-loss window: A acknowledges a replicated durable queue that remains transient authority until message-store commit and consumer ack; B acknowledges a replicated log quorum
463k routing lookups/s across 50M live connections: B's independently replayable persistence, fan-out, and push consumers scale and evolve without touching the acknowledgement path
peak = 4x average: B gives each concern independent lag, replay, and scaling controls rather than A's shared delivery-worker bottleneck
per-conversation ordering falls out of partition-by-conversation — the consistency target met by construction
the honest costs: B's operational skill floor and testability (2/5) are accepted for replayable consumers and evolvability; rejected C failed the no-acknowledged-loss invariant

risks.text: presence fan-out (status changes × friends) can exceed message volume — needs its own budget and viewport-scoped subscriptions
delivery-topic-per-gateway grows with fleet size; consumer rebalance storms during deploys
log retention vs 30-day offline queue: parked messages must move to the store, not live in the log
